Impel

/im-PEL/ - rhymes with bell · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Impel means to drive or urge someone forward to take action.

The smell of smoke impelled the night guard to leave his booth and check every floor.

Worked Example

A documentary on river plastic impelled fourteen-year-old Tessa to organize a monthly cleanup; by June, forty neighbors were hauling tires out of the shallows with her.

Impel is stronger than invite or encourage — it names a push you feel, from feelings or circumstances, that sets you moving. Notice the frame it demands: something impels someone to do something.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

drive: Drive is the everyday word for pushing someone toward an act, and it covers almost any pressure — ambition, fear, a deadline. Impel is its formal cousin and names the felt push itself, in a fixed frame: something impels someone to do something.

urge: To urge is to press someone with words and encouragement — a coach urges the team on. Impel needs no speaker at all: feelings or circumstances supply the push, and you can be impelled to act without anyone saying a word.

prod: A prod is a small, repeated poke toward action — reminders, pointed questions — and it is far gentler than impel. What impels you is one strong push you feel; what prods you just keeps tapping until you finally move.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

curb: to hold an urge or action back rather than push it forward

daunt: to drain someone's will to act — the push running in reverse

Where it sits · how much choice the pressure leaves — nudge → impel → compel

nudge vs. impel: A nudge is the gentlest push — a hint that you might act — and it stops well short of impel, which is real pressure that sets you moving.

compel vs. impel: Compel goes further than impel: what impels you presses you to act, but what compels you leaves no real choice at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-

Prefix — im-: in, into, against (a form of in-)

Root — -pel

Root — -pel: to push, to drive (Latin pellere)

Put it together

Put it together: Im- here is the directional twin of in- — 'in, into, against' — not the negative one, and -pel is Latin pellere, 'to drive.' To impel is literally to drive someone into motion. The same pel- pushes through propel, expel, and repel; nothing in this word means 'not.'

Use the root in a new word: propel

Use the root in a new word: propel: The little outboard motor propelled the raft across the lake faster than eight paddlers ever had.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal

Impel is a formal verb for the felt push that starts an action, and it keeps a fixed frame: something impels someone to do something. In everyday speech, prompt or push does the job. Its past form impelled has its own card next, and compel — its stronger cousin — leaves no choice at all.
